scene: Title card, then the guess-and-judge picture from the short video, shrunk to a corner.
caption: This is the long version. In short: AI models running on my own Macs write programs for Advent of Code puzzles, an exact automatic judge decides which are right, and I measure whether combining many attempts beats a single one, and by how much.

scene: The README pipeline, animated: puzzle → model → Python program → sandbox → oracle → ledger.
caption: For technical viewers: each puzzle goes to a large language model running locally through Ollama. The model writes a Python program. The program runs in a sandbox against the real puzzle input, and an oracle compares its output with the accepted answer. An overfit gate rejects programs that just copy the example's numbers.
say: For technical viewers: each puzzle goes to a large language model running locally through Ollama. The model writes a Python program. The program runs in a sandbox against the real puzzle input, and an oracle compares its output with the accepted answer. An overfit gate rejects programs that just copy the example's numbers.

scene: Strategy layer lights up over the loop: several drafts, repair arrow, fallback model, vote.
caption: On top of that loop sit the strategies I wanted to measure: drawing several drafts instead of one, repairing a failed draft using its own error, switching to a second model, and voting among answers when no answer key exists.

scene: One run: 0 of 2, red. Three repeat trials of the same setup: 6 of 6, green.
caption: Every setup gets a fingerprint, every experiment runs several trials, and every attempt is recorded, solved or not. The models are random, so one run says almost nothing. I learned that the hard way: a single test once returned 0 out of 2 and looked exactly like a broken upgrade. Three trials of the same setup gave 6 out of 6.

I learned that the hard way: a single test once returned zero out of two and looked exactly like a broken upgrade. Three trials of the same setup gave six out of six.

scene: Three columns: local models (guess), AI assistants (build), scripts (judge). This segment fills the first.
caption: Who does what is deliberate. The models under test all run locally, on my own Macs. That makes each attempt essentially free, so I could afford thousands of them. It keeps the puzzle data private. And a local model is frozen by its exact version, so it can't change underneath an experiment the way a cloud service can.

scene: Second column fills: AI coding assistants writing the harness, analysis scripts, docs; a line from them to the judge is crossed out.
caption: I built the platform with AI coding assistants as engineering partners: writing and restructuring the harness, writing the analysis scripts, and checking every written claim against the data. But no AI ever decides whether a puzzle was solved.

scene: Third column fills: oracle, verify_solutions (69/69), recompute_results --check (22/22 claims).
caption: That job belongs to scripts, because it has to be exact. The oracle runs the code and compares answers. One script re-checks all 69 recorded solutions; another recomputes every number I publish from the raw results and fails the build if one drifts. Guesses where a guess is good enough, exact checks wherever truth matters: the same pattern as the solver itself.
say: That job belongs to scripts, because it has to be exact. The oracle runs the code and compares answers. One script re-checks all sixty-nine recorded solutions; another recomputes every number I publish from the raw results and fails the build if one drifts. Guesses where a guess is good enough, exact checks wherever truth matters: the same pattern as the solver itself.

scene: Timeline begins: Dec 2024, 16 GB laptop, small models; scattered dots of single runs.
caption: It began in December 2024 on a 16-gigabyte laptop with small models. The first lesson there was that single runs are noise, so repeated A/B tests became the rule.
say: It began in December twenty twenty-four on a sixteen-gigabyte laptop with small models. The first lesson there was that single runs are noise, so repeated A B tests became the rule.

scene: Timeline: August 2026, 32 GB machine, a 27-billion-parameter model sweeps the small models' failures.
caption: In August 2026, a newer 27-billion-parameter model on a 32-gigabyte machine solved what the small models couldn't, and the real question came into focus: does coordinating attempts keep its value as models get stronger?
say: In August twenty twenty-six, a newer twenty-seven-billion-parameter model on a thirty-two-gigabyte machine solved what the small models couldn't, and the real question came into focus: does coordinating attempts keep its value as models get stronger?

scene: Five ideas tested in a row, each crossed out; a filter icon appears: 'new information?'
caption: Then five ideas failed in a row. None of them gave the model any information it didn't already have, and that became my filter for what to try next.

scene: A Part 2 prompt with the Part 1 story missing; it slides back in. Bars: 6/20 → 19/19; 2/53 → 29/37.
caption: The biggest finding was about my own harness, not strategy. Each puzzle has two parts, and my prompts for Part 2 left out the Part 1 story it builds on, so the model had to guess the rules. On one puzzle, restoring that context and nothing else took it from 6 out of 20 to 19 out of 19. On 13 Part 2s the model had failed, it went from 2 in 53 to 29 in 37. Those 13 were picked because they had failed, and two smaller settings changed too, but what looked like a wall in the model was mostly missing information.

scene: Curve of one-draft rate vs three-draft gain: big in the middle, flat at the ends. Predicted 52%, measured 49%.
caption: Second, extra attempts pay off about as much as independent tries predict: in three tests, three drafts solved 49% where single-draft rates predicted 52%. So more attempts help most on problems the model solves sometimes. Under my original harness, they lifted those problems from 42% to 75%. After the fix, few problems were left in that middle band, and on the one that was, a repeat test I registered in advance could not confirm the lift.

So more attempts help most on problems the model solves sometimes. Under my original harness, they lifted those problems from forty-two to seventy-five percent. After the fix, few problems were left in that middle band, and on the one that was, a repeat test I registered in advance could not confirm the lift.

scene: Two models on one problem: 10/10 vs 1/10. Repair: 17 of 427. A correct-but-slow program hits the clock.
caption: Third, a second model helped by being chosen, not mixed in: one solved a problem 10 times in 10 that my reference model solved once in 10. And repairing a failed draft rarely rescued it, 17 times in 427. The hardest failures were programs that were right but too slow.
say: Third, a second model helped by being chosen, not mixed in: one solved a problem ten times in ten that my reference model solved once in ten. And repairing a failed draft rarely rescued it, seventeen times in four hundred twenty-seven. The hardest failures were programs that were right but too slow.

scene: Twelve defect cards stack up; the corpus totals count up beside them.
caption: Underneath it all: measurement is most of the work. I found twelve defects in my own instruments, each of which made results look better or worse than they were. In all: 125 experiment runs, 3,842 attempts, about 235 GPU-hours and 48.2 million tokens.

In all: a hundred twenty-five experiment runs, three thousand eight hundred forty-two attempts, about two hundred thirty-five G P U hours and forty-eight million tokens.

scene: Timeline: model release dates, then the 2024–2025 puzzles shaded 'seen?'; Dec 1 2026 beyond them, clean.
caption: One caveat hangs over all of this. The 2024 and 2025 puzzles are public and older than the models, so a model may have seen solutions while it was trained. Advent of Code 2026, starting December 1st, is the clean test: puzzles published after every model I use.

scene: A Mac at night: 02:00, run starts, answers submitted from a separate account, budget meter.
caption: I registered the plan in advance, and froze the model, prompts and settings. Each night of the event, five hours after the puzzle is released, a scheduled run on my Mac attempts it from a separate account and submits answers under a fixed budget of wrong guesses, outside the race. It also tests my biggest caveat: does the Part 1 context help because it informs, or because it reminds the model of something it memorized?

scene: The exact judge fades to a weaker one (worked example only): 15 of 35 trials pick a wrong program.
caption: After that comes the real goal: problems beyond puzzles. Most real problems have no answer key. My first data shows what that costs: judging by the puzzle's worked example alone picked a wrong program in 15 of 35 trials. How much coordination still helps with weaker checks is the next question.
